_comment: Per-Actor execution policy. Every field is optional; an Actor with no entry is bounded only by the Worker's global --concurrency and by the 'defaults' section. LIMITS (security review H-03, 2026-10-23): each Actor has a 'limits' section -- a default and a maximum for the wall-clock timeout, memory and CPUs, a process cap, and for browser Actors a /dev/shm size. The defaults were chosen from a review of all 2,598 past runs (scripts/review_run_limits.py): the default timeout is at least 2.5x the longest successful run of that Actor, rounded up; the maximum is about 3x the default. Memory had never been measured, so it is generous -- browser Actors 3 GB, the rest 1-2 GB -- and every run now records its peak so these can be tightened from data. A run may ask for other values up to the maximum (console 'Run options', or ?timeout_minutes=&memory_mb=&cpus= on POST /actors/{name}/runs). The Worker's own --cpus/--memory flags stay as a host-wide ceiling above all of this.

global.note: NOT RAISED. With per-run memory limits in place the arithmetic is now possible: six concurrent runs at the largest default (3 GB) is 18 GB of LIMITS on this 14 GB host, but limits are ceilings, not reservations, and the measured peaks recorded from now on are what should decide whether to raise this. Users seeing 'queued' is honest and is what the queue is for; per-user quotas (ACTOR_PLATFORM_MAX_ACTIVE_RUNS_PER_USER) keep one account from filling it.

defaults.limits_note: Applies WHOLE to any Actor without its own 'limits' section (a new Actor, say). Modest on purpose: an unknown Actor should have to ask for more.

hello_world.note: A platform test fixture, not a scraper. HIDDEN from human-facing clients so nobody picks it while looking for something to scrape -- but deliberately NOT deleted: this Actor and item_processor are the fixtures 20+ suites run against, and removing them would leave the platform with no way to test itself that does not hit a real website.
hello_world.limits_note: Test fixture. Longest of 1,284 successful runs: 2 s. Ten minutes is far beyond anything it does, and the suites that exercise long runs ask for more explicitly.

item_processor.note: The other test fixture -- it fails part way through on purpose, to exercise failure handling. Hidden for the same reason, and kept for the same reason.
item_processor.limits_note: Test fixture. Longest of 380 successful runs: 7 s.

linkedin.label: LinkedIn
linkedin.note: One run per CONNECTED ACCOUNT, like the other session-bearing Actors: two concurrent scrapes on one session make a single account look automated, while scrapes on different people's sessions are not in each other's way. Note this Actor's comment stage needs no session at all -- it reads each post's public page anonymously -- so the cap is really about the post feed.
linkedin.session_note: ONE cookie listed, and NO session_id_cookie. The jar also needs JSESSIONID (it is the CSRF token, echoed into a header on every API request), but only li_at is evidence of being logged IN -- which is what this list decides, since it guards both capture and the write-back. A jar that reaches the auth wall keeps JSESSIONID and loses li_at, so listing both would accept a dead session as a live one. There is NO account-identifying cookie in this jar at all, which is why session_id_cookie is absent: a connected account here shows no id, and that is the platform being honest rather than inventing one.
linkedin.limits_note: 13 successful runs: longest 415 s (a cancelled one ran 753 s). --deep-comments costs 30-50 s per post, which is what the 2-hour maximum is for. Drives Chromium.

tiktok.label: TikTok
tiktok.note: One run per CONNECTED ACCOUNT. Demo build: the collector returns synthetic data, so no browser, CAPTCHA or display is involved.
tiktok.session_note: ONE cookie, and NO session_id_cookie, for the same reasons as the other Meta-shaped jar: only this cookie proves a live session, while the CSRF token and device ids are handed to logged-OUT visitors too, so requiring them would let a bounced run pass as live. The cookie that names the account is optional in the jar and session_id_cookie must be one of session_cookies, so it is left unset rather than made able to refuse a working session.
tiktok.state_note: A durable per-account directory mounted at /actor/state. The real collector kept its browser profile there; the demo build only demonstrates the mount.
tiktok.limits_note: Same limits the real Actor ran under.

threads.label: Threads
threads.note: Session OPTIONAL, and it is the only Actor here for which that is true. Posts and a sample of replies are served to anyone, so a run with no connected account is never refused; a connected one lifts the reply ceiling, which anonymity cannot. No concurrency scope: an anonymous run shares nothing, and the authenticated reply query is a read that does not rotate its own cookies.
threads.platform_note: Sign-in is optional. Without it you get posts and only ~10-26 replies per post; connect an account to collect replies in full.
threads.session_note: ONE cookie listed and NO session_id_cookie, for the reason every other Meta-shaped jar here gives: only sessionid proves a live session, while csrftoken, mid and ig_did are handed to logged-OUT visitors too, so requiring them would refuse valid jars and accepting them as proof would pass a dead session as live. session_optional STAYS TRUE, and that is load-bearing: it is what keeps the API from demanding a connected account before a run, which would break the anonymous path this collector was built on. NO session_out: unlike the other five, this collector's auth.py is READ-ONLY -- it has no save_storage_state -- so there is nothing to write back and declaring the capability would promise one. THIS ENTRY USED TO SAY 'Do NOT be tempted to add a session', because a jar once took the same profile scrape from 25 posts to ZERO, silently. That hazard was real and is now fixed upstream rather than avoided: engine.py keeps a session-bearing client and a cookie-free one and hands each tier the right one, so the GraphQL feed and the SSR reply fallback never see a cookie. Verified live before enabling this -- 50 posts AND 1,188 replies in one authenticated run, posts stage not zeroed. If those two clients are ever merged, this must go back to being un-connectable.
threads.limits_note: 21 successful runs: longest 112 s. But an authenticated 'collect ALL comments' run was measured at 51.8 min for 50 posts, so the maximum covers that. httpx only.

x.label: X
x.note: One run per CONNECTED ACCOUNT, like the other session-bearing Actors. Worth knowing that this site's limits are per 15-minute window and generous (50 timeline calls, 150 conversation calls), so the cap here is about not racing one account's session write-back rather than about rate limits.
x.session_note: ONE cookie listed, and NO session_id_cookie. The jar also needs the CSRF token, echoed into a header on every request and rejected on a mismatch -- but that token is handed to logged-OUT visitors too, so requiring it would let a jar that hit the login wall pass as a live session and let the write-back overwrite a good stored session with a dead one. The cookie that would NAME the account is optional in the jar, and session_id_cookie must be one of session_cookies, so it is left unset rather than made able to refuse a working session.
x.limits_note: 3 successful runs: longest 57 s; a 50-post, 1,000-reply run is ~2.5 min. Playwright is in the image for the hashtag path, so it is sized as a browser Actor.

instagram.label: Instagram
instagram.note: One run per CONNECTED ACCOUNT, like the other session-bearing Actors: the site rotates its session cookie server-side during a run, so two concurrent scrapes on the SAME session race the write-back and make the account look automated. Two scrapes on two different people's sessions are not in each other's way.
instagram.session_note: ONE cookie, and NO session_id_cookie -- both deliberate. Only this cookie is evidence of a live session; the others in the jar (csrftoken, ds_user_id, mid, ig_did) are set for logged-out visitors too, so requiring them would prove nothing while refusing valid jars. The cookie that would NAME the account is optional in the jar, and session_id_cookie must be one of session_cookies (the account id must come from a jar that was accepted as a session) -- so naming it here would either make a display nicety able to refuse a working session, or, if this cookie were used instead, publish the session credential itself as the account's visible id. A connected account with no id shown is the correct trade.
instagram.limits_note: 6 successful runs: longest 507 s. Drives Chromium, hence 3 GB, a high process cap (Chrome counts every thread) and a 1 GB /dev/shm.

facebook_groups.label: Facebook Groups
facebook_groups.note: NO session, NO login, NO connected account, and no concurrency scope - this Actor collects PUBLIC groups only, over plain HTTP, holding no credentials of any kind. Two runs cannot be in each other's way because neither holds a session to race. It is bounded only by the Worker's global limit.
facebook_groups.platform_note: No sign-in needed - this Actor reads only what a logged-out visitor can see on a public group. A private group is reported as private rather than attempted.
facebook_groups.session_note: requires_social is deliberately ABSENT, and that is not an oversight. Naming a platform here makes the API demand a connected account, and naming the SAME platform as another Actor whose session policy differs makes the shared policy loader raise - which would break the account picker for every Actor at once, not just this one. This Actor needs no account, so it names no platform and stays un-connectable by construction. Do NOT add a session to it: the scrape is answered anonymously, and there is nothing a cookie jar would unlock that is not also a different Actor's job.
facebook_groups.limits_note: 6 successful runs: longest 660 s. A full 1,000-post public run pages ~235 times (~7 min) before up to 20 comments per post, so 60 min with a 3-hour maximum. httpx only.

facebook.label: Facebook Pages
facebook.note: One run per CONNECTED ACCOUNT, not one run per Actor. The site rotates its session cookie server-side during a run, so two concurrent scrapes on the SAME session race the write-back and make the account look automated. Two scrapes on two different people's sessions are not in each other's way, so capping the Actor throttled thirty users to serialise a constraint that only ever applied to one. It is policy here rather than a lock inside the scraper because the scraper implements no cap at all.
facebook.session_note: Which cookies prove a live session, and which one names the account. BOTH of session_cookies are required: c_user survives a logout, so a jar with it and no xs looks like a login and is not one -- capturing on c_user alone stores a session that fails on first use. They live here rather than in platform code because no Actor may be named in worker/, api/, jobqueue/ or registry/; test_facebook.py enforces that by grep.
facebook.limits_note: 58 successful runs: median 32 s, 95th percentile 256 s, longest 2,880 s (48 min: a group, 10-day window, with comments). 120 min is 2.5x that; month-long group windows with comments take hours, hence a 6-hour maximum. httpx only -- no browser in the image -- but a big group run holds thousands of posts and comments in memory, so 2 GB.
